parts.ask: A particle of mass km is fixed at A on the rim of the plane face of a uniform solid hemisphere (mass m, radius a, centre O); the loaded solid rests with its curved surface on a horizontal plane and OA at α to the horizontal, tan α = √3: find the exact value of k
parts.ms: M1A1 (k + 1)m x̄ = kma, so x̄ = ka/(k + 1); A1 ȳ = 3a/(8(k + 1)); M1 tan α = x̄/ȳ, trig the right way, solve; A1 3√3/8. Alt: moments about O, m(3a/8) sin α = kma cos α (MS pp.11–12)

parts.ask: Show that t = (a + √(bx² + c))/d, where a, b, c and d are integers to be found

parts.ask: P (mass m) hangs in equilibrium at O on a light elastic string (natural length a, modulus 3mg/4) fixed at A: find OA
parts.ms: M1 resolve vertically with Hooke's law, extension 4a/3; A1 7a/3 (MS pp.15–16)

parts.ask: P is pulled down to B with AB = 3a and released from rest: show that throughout the subsequent motion P performs only simple harmonic motion, justifying the answer
parts.final_form: ẍ = −(3g/4a)x, and the string never goes slack
parts.ms: M1A1 equation of motion with weight and tension, variable measured from equilibrium; DM1A1 ẍ = −(3g/4a)x, hence SHM; B1 amplitude 2a/3; B1 2a/3 < 4a/3 (the equilibrium extension), so the string stays taut and the motion is always SHM (MS pp.15–16)

parts.ask: C is vertically below A with AC = 2a: find, in terms of a and g, the speed of P as it passes through C
parts.ms: M1A1ft v² = (3g/4a)[(2a/3)² − (a/3)²]; A1 cso. Alt: energy with 2 EPE terms, GPE and KE (MS pp.15–16)

parts.ask: Find the time taken for P to move directly from B to C
parts.ms: M1A1ft x = (2a/3) cos ωt with x = −a/3, so cos ωt = −1/2; DM1 complete method for t; A1 any correct equivalent. Note: the scheme prints [14] as the question total; the question paper and the part marks give 15 (MS pp.15–16)

parts.ask: P (mass m) on a light inextensible string of length 8a fixed at O on a smooth horizontal desk (edge point E with OE = 5a); held at A, 8a vertically above O, and projected horizontally at √(8ag) in the direction OE; above the level of OE it moves on a vertical circle of radius 8a: show the tension at angle θ to the upward vertical is T = 3mg(1 − cos θ)
parts.ms: M1A1A1 energy at a general point, two KE terms and the GPE change, v² = 24ga − 16ga cos θ; M1A1 radial T + mg cos θ = mv²/(8a); DM1 eliminate v; A1* (MS pp.17–18)

parts.ask: When the string is horizontal P passes through B: find the instantaneous change in tension as P passes through B (the string then turns about the edge E)
parts.ms: B1 v_B² = 24ga (not implied by just using (a)); B1 tension for either radius, 3mg (radius 8a) or 8mg (radius 3a); B1 ΔT = 5mg (MS pp.17–18)

parts.ask: P hits the vertical side EF of the desk, rebounds losing one third of its kinetic energy, and in the subsequent motion the string goes slack at angle α to the upward vertical through O: show cos α = 7/12
parts.ms: M1 energy to the wall, v₁² = 30ag; A1 after impact v₂² = 20ag; M1A1 energy to the slack point, ½m(20ag) − mg(3a) = ½mv² + mg(8a cos α); M1 radial equation with T = 0, mg cos α = mv²/(8a); A1 equation in cos α; A1* (MS pp.17–18)

parts.ms: M1 inverse-square relation F = k/(x + R)² (k = GMm allowed); dM1 x = 0 with F = mg to find k; A1* positive (MS pp.9, 11)

parts.ask: A particle released from rest above the surface has speed U at height R: find, in terms of U, g and R, its speed when it strikes the surface

parts.ms: B1 cos θ = 4/5, sin θ = 3/5; B1 ω = π; M1A1 vertical T_A cos θ − T_B cos θ = 600g; M1A1 horizontal (T_A + T_B) sin θ = 600ω²(5 sin θ), radius 3 substituted; dM1 solve simultaneously; A1 T_A; A1 T_B (MS pp.12–13)

parts.ask: In a refined model both arms stretch to 5.1 m: state how this affects the sum of the tensions, justifying the answer

parts.ms: B1 mass ratio (2/3)πr³ : (1/3)πr²(kr); B1 centres 3r/8 and kr/4 from the common plane face; M1 moments with combined centre of mass at O (the centre of the plane face), ignore signs; A1ft correct equation; A1 k = √3 exact. parts.ask: P (mass m) on a light inextensible string of length a, held with OA horizontal and projected vertically downwards with speed √(9ag/5); when the string makes angle θ with the downward vertical the tension is S: show S = (3/5)mg(5 cos θ + 3)
parts.ms: M1A1 radial equation S − mg cos θ = mv²/a (3 terms, weight resolved); M1A1 energy from A to the general position, difference of two KE terms and the PE change ("M0 for v² = u² + 2as"); DM1 eliminate v²; A1* cso (MS p.16)

parts.ask: At the instant the string becomes slack the speed of P is v: show v = √(3ag/5)
parts.ms: B1 cos θ = −3/5 from S = 0; M1 use it to find v² or v; A1* (MS p.16)

parts.ask: Find the maximum height of P above the horizontal level of O
parts.ms: M1 vertical component of velocity at slack, √(3ag/5) × 4/5 (sin/cos confusion allowed); M1 vertical distance to the top with that component; A1 24a/125; A1ft add 3a/5 (both M needed). Alts: energy from the slack point, or from A, with only the horizontal component left at the top (MS pp.16–17)

parts.ms: M1 equate the two Hooke's-law tensions, 20(1)/2 = λ(0.8)/1.2; A1 correct; A1* (MS p.18)

parts.ask: P is projected towards B; x is the displacement from O: show that while both strings are taut ẍ = −18x
parts.ms: M1 N2L for P with both tensions (acceleration may be written a); A1 at most one error; A1 fully correct, e.g. 1.25ẍ = 15(0.8 − x)/1.2 − 20(1 + x)/2; A1* (MS p.18)

parts.ask: Initial speed 10 m/s: find the speed of P when the string PB becomes slack
parts.ms: B1 amplitude a = 10/√18 (= 5√2/3) oe; M1 v² = ω²(a² − x²) with x = 0.8; A1 9.4 or 9.41. Alt: energy with 3 EPE and 2 KE terms (MS pp.18–19)

parts.ask: Both strings are taut for T seconds in one complete oscillation: find T
parts.ms: M1A1A1 time from O to x = 0.8 (PB slack), 0.8 = (10/√18) sin √18 t₁; M1A1 time from O to x = −1 (PA slack); A1 T = 2(t₁ + t₂) = 0.37. Consistent degrees allowed for the intermediate times; alternatives must be complete methods. Alt: x = a cos ωt with T = 2(t₂ − t₁) (MS pp.18–19)

parts.ms: M1 π∫(1 + √x)² dx, π required; A1 x + (4/3)x^(3/2) + x²/2; A1* limits seen, "Must include units"; missing units penalised at most once per question (MS p.7)

parts.ask: Show that the centre of mass of S is 49/85 m from O
parts.ms: M1 π∫x(1 + √x)² dx; A1 x²/2 + (4/5)x^(5/2) + x³/3; A1 49/30 (with or without π); dM1 divide by the volume, π in both or neither; A1* "Must include units" (MS p.7)

parts.ask: Calculator warning. P moves on the x-axis with v = (2x + 1)^(3/2) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2/3, through O at t = 0: find x when the acceleration is 243 m s⁻²
parts.ms: M1 a = v dv/dx or d(½v²)/dx, power down by 1; A1 3(2x + 1)²; M1 (independent) set equal to 243 and solve; A1 x = 4, "If -5 is seen then it must be rejected" (MS p.10)
parts.er: Most used v dv/dx. Commonest error: differentiating v with respect to x only (still 1 method mark for equating to 243). The final mark was occasionally lost by keeping the extra root: the ER prints "included x = 4 in their solution", evidently meaning −5, which the MS says must be rejected (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Find v in terms of t
parts.ms: M1A1 dx/dt = (2x + 1)^(3/2) (or dv/dt = 3v^(5/3)); M1 separate and integrate; A1 −(2x + 1)^(−1/2) = t + C; M1 t = 0, x = 0 gives C, equation in v and t; A1. "No marks in (b) for use of a = 243" (MS p.10)
parts.er: Calculus and algebra separated the grades. Many reached (2x + 1)^(−1/2) = 1 − t but then solved for x and used the quotient rule instead of seeing they were nearly done (ER p.4). General comments: some candidates may have spent too long on 4(b), and the Q7 comments suggest this cost time at the end of the paper (ER pp.3, 5)

parts.ask: P (mass m) hangs from A by a string of length a√3 and from B (AB = a, B vertically below A) by a string of length a, moving in a horizontal circle with angular speed ω with both strings taut: show that the upper string is at 30° and the lower at 60° to the downward vertical
parts.ms: M1 cosine rule on triangle APB or trig on half of it; A1* "Stating OBP = 2 OAP alone is not sufficient" (MS p.11)
parts.er: Simple geometry, but many lacked clear communication: angles called θ or α with no indication of where they were; presentation poor (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Show that the tension in the upper string is ½m√3(2g − aω²)
parts.ms: M1A1 vertical T_A cos 30° + T_B cos 60° = mg; M1A1A1 horizontal T_A sin 30° + T_B sin 60° = mrω² ("If rω² is never seen, this is an A error"); B1 r = a sin 60°; dM1 solve for T_A; A1* "Must see exactly" (MS p.11)
parts.er: Answered very well; correct form of acceleration and few sin/cos errors. Some lost the last mark by not stating the answer exactly as printed (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Show that 2g/(3a) < ω² < 2g/a
parts.ms: M1 use T_A > 0 or T_B > 0 for one inequality; A1; M1 use both (T_B = (3/2)maω² − mg); A1* (MS p.11)
parts.er: Many assumed solving T_A = 0 and T_B = 0 was enough. State the conditions as inequalities, T_A > 0 and T_B > 0, at the start; both were needed for the method marks (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Small smooth ring R (mass m) on a smooth circular wire (centre O, radius l) in a vertical plane, attached by an elastic string (natural length l, modulus mg) to the lowest point A; R is slightly disturbed from the top and reaches B with OB horizontal, speed v: show that v² = 2gl√2
parts.ms: B1 KE and GPE difference (½mv² − mgl); M1 EPE formula; A1 top EPE mgl²/(2l); A1 at B mg(l√2 − l)²/(2l); M1 energy with 1 GPE, 1 KE and 2 EPE terms; dM1 solve for v²; A1* exact (MS p.12)
parts.er: One of the hardest: a fifth scored zero. Some did not recognise an EPE question and tried Hooke's law and tension, then abandoned; those using energy with both EPE terms, GPE and KE usually succeeded (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Show that the magnitude of the force exerted on R by the wire at B is N = ½mg(5√2 − 2)
parts.ms: M1A1 Hooke's law at B, T = mg(√2 − 1); M1A1A1 horizontal N2L at B, N + T cos 45° = mv²/l; dM1 substitute T and v²; A1* if N comes out negative, use of "magnitude" or modulus must justify the printed answer (MS p.12)
parts.er: Many who did (a) made no attempt. An equation of motion horizontally at B was needed; some wrote an equilibrium equation instead; for some the only marks were the 2 for Hooke's law at B (ER p.5)

parts.ask: P (mass m) on a smooth table between two springs, each natural length l: to A modulus 2mg, to B modulus mg, AB = 4l; equilibrium at O with AO = 5l/3; P is moved l/2 from O towards A and released: show that P moves with SHM of period T = 2π√(l/(3g))
parts.ms: M1 N2L at a general position, T_A − T_B = mẍ; dM1 Hooke's law, extensions different and of the form (d ± x); A1 a for acceleration allowed; A1 with ẍ, SHM; M1 2π/ω; A1* cso including the SHM conclusion (MS p.13)
parts.er: Only question with modal score zero; a fifth scored nothing, even high achievers struggled. Many reached ẍ = −ω²x but did not conclude "SHM" (ER pp.5–6)

parts.ask: Find the speed of P as it passes through O
parts.ms: B1 (l/2)√(3g/l) o.e., positive; isw on later surd simplification (MS p.13)
parts.er: SHM formulae well known: those who failed (a) could still use the printed period to find ω and score (b) and (c) (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the maximum acceleration of P
parts.ms: B1 "Max acceleration so must be positive" (MS p.13)
parts.er: The mark was occasionally lost for giving the maximum acceleration as a negative value (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the exact time from release until P is first moving with speed (3/4)√(gl)
parts.ms: M1 x = a cos ωt so v = −aω sin ωt; M1 equation in t with a = l/2, ω = √(3g/l); A1; M1 solve; A1. Alts: sin form then ¼ period − t; v² = ω²(a² − x²) then x = l/4. SC: amplitude ½ used throughout caps (d) at M1M1A0M0A0 (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: Those who understood used x = a cos ωt and scored 5/5 in a few lines; v² = ω²(a² − x²) also worked; x = a sin ωt was valid but rarely completed (time must be subtracted from ¼ period) (ER p.6)

parts.ms: B1 mass ratios H : h : H − h (πr²/3 cancelled); B1 distances 3H/4, H − h/4, x̄ (another axis allowed); M1 moments, solids not shells; A1; A1* with (H − h) cancelled; "A factorised expression should be seen" (MS pp.9–10)
parts.er: Well understood. Many kept full volume expressions instead of the ratio H : h : H − h. Some jumped from the moments equation to the printed answer without manipulation; working must show how it is reached (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Car on a track banked at α moves in a horizontal circle of radius r; at speed ½√(gr) there is no sideways friction: show that tan α = 1/4
parts.ms: M1A1 R cos α = mg; M1A1 R sin α = m(gr/4)/r ("Allow rω² for acceleration but not 'a'"); or M2A2 N2L down the slope; A1* exactly as printed. Using μ instead of α in (a) loses only the last mark (MS p.11)
parts.er: First major challenge: a quarter scored nothing. Many wrote expressions, not equations, then the answer; F used for friction, centripetal force and ma alike. Misconception: R = mg cos α (equilibrium perpendicular to the plane) (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Sideways friction has coefficient μ (μ < 4); V is the maximum speed without slipping: find V in terms of μ, r and g
parts.ms: M1A1 vertical (or perpendicular) equation S cos α − F sin α = mg ("M0 if R from (a) is used"); M1A1 horizontal (or parallel) N2L S sin α + F cos α = mV²/r; B1 F = μS; dM1 eliminate F, substitute the trig, solve; A1 (MS pp.11–12)
parts.er: Friction caused major difficulty; 1 or 0 marks common. The normal reaction is not the same as in (a), yet reusing R was common, as was substituting mg cos α at once. Set up the basic equations before substituting F or R (ER p.5). General comments: Q4 was the least familiar context and challenged even high achievers; 4(b) lacked clarity and fluency (ER p.3)

parts.ask: P is projected vertically up with speed U from the surface of the Earth (fixed sphere, centre O, radius R); its acceleration is gR²/x² towards O at distance x: show that v² = 2gR²/x + U² − 2gR
parts.ms: M1A1 v dv/dx = −gR²/x² (any derivative form for the M, minus sign for the A); M1 separate and integrate; A1 ½v² = gR²/x + C; M1 x = R, v = U for C; A1*. Energy alternative must use integration of the variable force (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: Well answered at all levels. Energy attempts rarely succeeded because calculus was not used for the work done. Good technique: rewriting the final answer to match the printed form; sign slips fixed by returning to the first line (ER p.5)

parts.ask: P first moves with speed ½√(gR) at B; given U = √(gR), find the distance AB in terms of R
parts.final_form: AB = 3R/5 (distance from the surface, not from O)
parts.ms: M1 substitute into (a); A1 x = 8R/5; A1 3R/5 (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: Most common error: leaving 8R/5 instead of subtracting the radius R; distances are measured from the centre of the Earth (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the smallest value of U that ensures P never comes to rest, explaining your reasoning
parts.ms: M1 a statement about 2gR²/x: positive for x ≥ R, or → 0 as x → ∞; dM1 correct reasoning giving U² − 2gR ≥ 0 (or U² → 2gR); A1 cso (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: Many made no attempt. Many stated √(2gR) without mathematical reasoning; the term 2gR²/x had to be dealt with, usually by letting x tend to infinity; sufficient explanation challenged even high achievers (ER p.6)

parts.ask: P on a string of length a from O is held with the string taut and horizontal and projected vertically downwards with speed u; when the string has turned through θ, the tension is T: show that T = mu²/a + 3mg sin θ
parts.ms: M1A1A1 energy ½mv² − ½mu² = mga sin θ; M1A1A1 N2L towards O T − mg sin θ = mv²/a ("do not accept 'a'" for acceleration); A1* exactly as printed (MS pp.15–16)
parts.er: Answered very well; errors in the equation of motion came from a missing weight term. Some wrote the printed answer straight after the equations: show at least one step (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Given u = 2√(3ag/5), find the speed of P when the string goes slack
parts.ms: M1 T = 0 with u² = 12ag/5; A1 sin θ = −4/5; M1 energy (or T = 0 in the equation of motion) with their sin θ; A1 (MS pp.15–16)
parts.er: Most found sin θ and substituted correctly; errors came from the later algebra (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Hence find the maximum height of P above O in the subsequent motion
parts.ms: M1A1ft vertical motion 0 = (v cos θ)² − 2gh, or energy with the horizontal component kept ("A component of speed must be used"); A1 h = 18a/125; dM1 add 4a/5 (height of the slack point); A1 118a/125. Alt energy from the start M2A1ftA1A1 (MS pp.15–16)
parts.er: Distinguished grades; lower grades often abandoned it. Some found 18a/125 but forgot to add 4a/5; energy users assumed all KE became GPE, forgetting the horizontal component at the top; others missed the vertical component or confused sin/cos. A large clear diagram would help (ER pp.6–7)

parts.ask: P (mass m) on an elastic string (natural length l) hangs in equilibrium D below a ceiling; it is pulled down to 3l below the ceiling and released, and comes to instantaneous rest just before reaching the ceiling: show that D = 5l/3
parts.ms: M1A1 Hooke's law at equilibrium λ(D − l)/l = mg; M1A1A1 energy λ(2l)²/(2l) = mg(3l), EPE of the form λx²/(kl); A1* (MS pp.17–18)
parts.er: Modal score zero on this question, yet over 80% gained some marks. Hooke's law was usually right, but many did not see an energy equation was needed and wrote incorrect working then the printed answer (ER p.7)

parts.ask: Show that, while the string is stretched, P moves with SHM with period 2π√(2l/(3g))
parts.ms: M1 N2L at a general position; dM1 Hooke's law with extension measured from equilibrium (2l/3 + x); A1; A1 ẍ form with x-double-dot and SHM concluded; M1 period 2π/ω; A1* at least one line of working before the printed period (MS pp.17–18)
parts.er: Standard bookwork, often 5/6: many reached ẍ = −ω²x but used it only as a step to the period and did not conclude "SHM", losing a mark. Candidates who struggled with (a) often skipped (b) and (c); they should attempt parts after a given answer (ER p.7)

parts.ask: Find the exact time from release until the string first goes slack
parts.ms: M1 complete method, e.g. −2l/3 = (4l/3) cos ωt (sin approach needs ¼ period + t; cos with + needs ½ period − t), the correct ω; A1 at most one error; A1; A1 cao. "Do not ISW" (MS pp.17–18)
parts.er: Most attempts followed the main scheme and scored 4/4 in a few lines; x = a sin ωt approaches rarely succeeded. A complete method usually adds to or subtracts from a fraction of the period (ER p.7)

parts.ask: Spacecraft S (mass m) moves straight towards the centre O of a planet (radius R) under gravitational force mgR²/(2x²) at distance x ≥ R: show that v² = gR²/x + C
parts.ms: M1 differential equation in v and x with v dv/dx ("Cannot get this mark using t"); M1 separate and integrate; A1* at least one line between the integral and the answer, correct signs throughout. Starting from ½v² = −∫… scores M0M1A0*. Alt: work-energy with the integral of the force (MS p.7)
parts.er: Very good response. Some lost a mark by not treating it as "show that": starting the proof with v² = … ; candidates had to form a differential equation in v and x and separate the variables (ER p.4)

parts.ask: When x = 3R, v = √(3gR): find the speed of S when it hits the surface of the planet
parts.final_form: v = √(11gR/3) (accept √(33gR)/3), in terms of g and R
parts.ms: M1 use x = 3R, v² = 3gR to find C; A1 C = 8gR/3; A1 √(11gR/3). Alt: definite integral (MS pp.7–8)
parts.er: Very successful; most found the constant from (a); the rare definite-integral attempts were equally successful (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Light elastic spring (natural length l, modulus λ) from A on a smooth plane inclined at θ (tan θ = 5/12); P (mass m) released from rest at B, AB = 2l down the line of greatest slope, first comes to rest at C with AC = 0.7l: use conservation of mechanical energy to show that λ = 100mg/91
parts.ms: M1 GPE change mg(1.3l) sin θ = 0.5mgl; B1 one correct EPE term, λl²/(2l) or λ(0.3l)²/(2l); M1 energy equation B to C, all terms; A1; A1* evidence of simplification needed (MS p.9)
parts.er: Most successful question on the paper; cos for sin in the GPE term was rare. Advice: give at least one line of working or simplification between the energy equation and the printed answer (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Find the acceleration of P when it is released from rest at B
parts.final_form: a = 5g/7 (accept 0.71g or better; 7 if g = 9.8 used)
parts.ms: M1 N2L along the plane T − mg sin θ = ma; A1; A1 Hooke's law T = λ (extension l) substituted; A1 5g/7. g = 9.81 penalised once per question; "SHM equations can only be used if the motion is proven to be SHM first" (MS p.9)
parts.er: Mostly correct. Using g = 9.81 is not accepted on mechanics papers and lost the final mark when substituted before reaching the expression in g (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Region under y = ¼x(3 − x) from x = 0 to x = 2 rotated about the x-axis forms a uniform solid S of volume 2π/5: use algebraic integration to show that the x-coordinate of its centre of mass is 31/24
parts.ms: M1 π∫xy² dx with the curve substituted and integrated, (1/16)(9x³ − 6x⁴ + x⁵); A1 (1/16)(9x⁴/4 − 6x⁵/5 + x⁶/6); A1 limits 0 and 2 giving 31π/60 (value must be seen); M1 divide by the volume, π (and ρ) used consistently; A1* (MS p.10)
parts.er: Confident start, but some needlessly integrated to find the given volume. Integrals had to be evaluated before dividing: substituting the curve and writing the printed answer (a one-step calculator result) did not earn the marks (ER pp.4–5)

parts.ask: S is placed with its circular face on a rough plane inclined at α° and is on the point of toppling: find α
parts.ms: M1 tan α = y(2) / (2 − 31/24) = (½)/(17/24), reciprocal condoned; A1 12/17; A1 35, "A0 for use of radians" (MS p.10)
parts.er: The first real challenge on the paper: many could not form the relevant triangle. Those who labelled α on the figure usually identified the lengths and succeeded (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Particle moves in a horizontal circle of radius r on the rough inner surface (μ = ¼) of a fixed hollow cone, rim radius 4a, OV = 3a, vertex down: show that the maximum possible angular speed is √(16g/(13r))
parts.ms: M1A1A1 resolve vertically R sin θ = mg + F cos θ (friction down the slope for the maximum); M1A1A1 horizontal N2L R cos θ + F sin θ = mrω², any form of acceleration for the M; M1 F = μR used, not just quoted; DM1 substitute the trig (3-4-5) and solve (R = 20mg/13, F = 5mg/13); A1*. Alt: N2L parallel and perpendicular to the surface, the acceleration resolved (MS p.11)
parts.er: Routine and well prepared; friction the wrong way or sin/cos confusion was rare but cost at least 3 of the 9 marks. A misconception among weaker candidates: using μmg cos θ for friction (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Use algebraic integration to show that the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular disc of radius r is 4r/(3π) from the diameter (area of a circle πr² may be assumed)
parts.ms: M1 integral of the form k∫x√(r² − x²) dx (or ∫(r² − x²) dx about the other axis); A1 −(1/3)(r² − x²)^(3/2) or rx − x³/3; A1 limits giving (2/3)r³; M1 ½πr² x̄ = ∫…, ρ on both sides or neither; A1*. Parametric alternatives accepted (MS pp.12–13)
parts.er: Hard to get all the marks. Most used x² + y² = r²; parametric or polar attempts rarely succeeded; some needlessly integrated to find the given area; many solutions were poorly presented (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Lamina L is a semicircle of diameter AC = 8a, centre B; the semicircle on diameter AB is removed and attached to BC on the other side of AC, forming template T; d is the distance of the centre of mass of T from AC: show that d = 4a/π
parts.ms: B1 masses 8πa², 2πa², 2πa²; B1 distances 16a/(3π), 8a/(3π), −8a/(3π); M1 moments about AC (column vectors accepted once an equation is written); A1; A1* with some simplification (MS pp.13–14)
parts.er: More comfortable: neat tables or column vectors, but the M mark needs the moments equation taken out of the table or vectors; the final mark needs "d = 4a/π" stated (ER p.6)

parts.ask: T is freely suspended from A and hangs with AC at angle θ to the downward vertical: find the exact value of tan θ
parts.ms: M1 moments about an axis through A perpendicular to AC: 4a(8πa²) − 2a(2πa²) + 6a(2πa²) = 8πa² x̄; A1ft A1ft; A1 x̄ = 5a from A (a if measured from B); M1 tan θ = d/x̄; A1 4/(5π) only (MS p.14)
parts.er: Usually full marks for those who succeeded in (b). Marks lost for finding the angle θ without tan θ, and for using the distance from B instead of A (ER p.6)

parts.ask: A is vertically above B with AB = 3l; P (mass m) is joined to A and to B by two strings, each natural length l and modulus 4mg; P rests at E on the vertical line AEB: show that AE = 13l/8
parts.ms: M1 equilibrium with all three forces (weight and two tensions); A1 at most one error; A1; A1* "Must see AE =" (MS p.15)
parts.er: Most succeeded with the main method; the final mark needed the answer stated exactly as printed, AE = 13l/8 (ER p.6)

parts.ask: P is released from rest 2l below A; x is the downward displacement from E at time t: show that ẍ = −(8g/l)x
parts.ms: M1 N2L at a general position with all terms (both tensions in terms of 5l/8 ± x, 3l/8 ∓ x, and the weight), a for acceleration condoned; A1; A1; A1* must use ẍ (MS p.15)
parts.er: A challenge: many left out the weight in the equation of motion; apparent arrivals at the printed answer earned nothing without all forces. The correct form of acceleration was used almost always (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the speed of P when it is l/8 below E
parts.ms: M1 v² = ω²(a² − x²) with amplitude 3l/8 (or equivalent); A1 (8g/l)(9l²/64 − l²/64); A1 √(gl) only (MS p.15)
parts.er: Using the correct amplitude (3l/8) tripped many; a simple diagram helped. v² = ω²(a² − x²) or x = a cos ωt then differentiating both worked; rare energy approaches (5 terms) were usually right (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Find the length of time in each complete oscillation for which P is more than 1.5l from A
parts.final_form: (2/ω) cos⁻¹(−⅓) = cos⁻¹(−⅓)√(l/2g) ≈ 1.91√(l/2g) (≈ 1.35√(l/g)), in terms of g and l
parts.ms: B1 x = (3l/8) cos ωt (or sin) with the correct amplitude; M1 −l/8 = (3l/8) cos ωt (or sin form with the right adjustment); A1 equivalent exact or decimal forms accepted (MS p.16)
parts.er: Often left blank; few succeeded. Nearly all used a correct displacement formula and ω but could not adjust to the required time; the best answers drew a diagram or sin/cos sketch (ER pp.6–7)

parts.ask: Bowl made from part of a thin smooth spherical shell (centre O, radius r), rim horizontal and uppermost; rim point B where OB is at θ to the upward vertical, tan θ = 12/5; a ball projected horizontally with speed u from the lowest point A stays in contact until B, speed v: use energy to show v² = u² − (36/13)gr
parts.ms: M1 energy with all terms, height r + r cos θ; A1; A1* (MS p.17)
parts.er: Familiar; many scored 6 or 7 of 7 in (a)–(b). Sign errors were corrected by going back to the first line (ER p.7)

parts.ask: Show that u² ≥ (41/13)gr
parts.ms: M1 N2L towards O, R + mg cos θ = mv²/r (R = 0 condoned for the M); A1; M1 use R ≥ 0 and (a); A1* must state R ≥ 0; "If there is no reference to R, the max mark in (b) is M1A1M1A0*" (MS p.17)
parts.er: The last mark needed reference to the normal reaction: the inequality holds only because R ≥ 0. Stating v ≥ 0 is true but not a valid basis (ER p.7)

parts.ask: BC is a diameter of the rim; given u² = 4gr, use the model to show that after leaving the bowl at B the ball falls back into the bowl before reaching C
parts.final_form: conclusion in words: horizontal distance (≈ 0.87r) < BC = 24r/13 (≈ 1.85r), so it falls back into the bowl
parts.ms: B1 BC = 2r sin θ = 24r/13; M1A1 time to return to the level of B, t = 2v sin θ/g; M1A1 horizontal distance (v cos θ)t = 120v²/(169g), v² = 16gr/13; A1* comparison and conclusion. Alts: time to cross BC horizontally, or speed needed to reach C. Quoting the range formula correctly earns M1A1M1A1 (SC) (MS pp.17–18)
parts.er: Many creative approaches (at least seven). Marks lost for BC = 2r instead of 2r sin θ; a conclusion that the ball falls back in was always required. Presentation was poor: unstructured, mixing surds and g = 9.8; a diagram and labelled horizontal/vertical work helped (ER p.7)
